provenance.note: Filename carries no institution, shelfmark or folio. Identifying this image is the highest-value provenance task in the project: it is the only known group portrait of the three men.

images.description: Three men sit close together inside a pointed-arch niche, framed by a lapis border. At the left an old man with a full white beard, in a brown robe and a white turban wound over a green cap, leans forward and extends his right hand toward an open bifolium he holds at his knee — the gesture of a man explaining a diagram rather than presenting a gift. Beside him a black-bearded man in a lapis-blue robe and gold-crowned turban looks toward the same page. At the right a third man, red-bearded, in a deep green robe, sits half-turned away, listening rather than reading. Behind them a lilac panel is scattered with blue flowering sprays; gold arabesque fills the spandrels. The niche is set into dense tilework — a star-and-cross field in pale blue and orange above, a white strapwork ground studded with dark red rosettes below, divided by a course of salmon brick.
iconography: The open bifolium is the compositional centre: all three sightlines converge on it, and the eldest figure's hand is the only strong diagonal in the picture. The subject of the image is a document being explained.
Seating order reads as transmission: the elder explains, the second reads, the third listens. Whether or not the painter intended a lineage, that is what the arrangement encodes.

The green cap under the elder's turban is a marker of sayyid or scholarly status in Persianate painting; the gold-crowned turban on the central figure is grander, and the pairing is the picture's one quiet tension.

research.claim: Yazdī is Ibn Turka's disciple and closest associate, not a colleague — he attended his teacher's majālis, travelled with him to Herat, and looked after his children after his death.
research.source: Melvin-Koushki, The Quest for a Universal Science (Yale diss., 2012), 135–36

research.claim: Qāḍīzāda Rūmī directed the Samarkand Observatory, which places the central figure at the junction of the star science and the letter science.

The three men together represent the intellectual programme Melvin-Koushki calls the mathematicalization of the occult sciences: a lettrist, an astronomer-mathematician, and a historian who applied both to the interpretation of empire.
research.source: Melvin-Koushki, Powers of One, 1; Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists, 599

research.claim: A group portrait of these three specific men is iconographically unusual and may be a later commemorative construction rather than a contemporary likeness.

images.description: A full folio: four lines of nastaʿlīq above the painting, four below, all inside gold rules on cream paper gone tan at the edges. In the painting a seated figure in vermilion, white-turbaned with a green sash, faces a white-turbaned bearded man in blue over a dark red under-robe who receives with a raised hand. Behind them a hexagonal blue-green tile field and a panel of dark green foliage; a red architectural band caps the scene. Three attendants in red tāj caps stand at the left in orange, blue-spotted and gold robes. In the foreground a servant in gold kneels to present a dish, and a gold platter of gifts sits on a pink floral carpet. Outside the composition, at the lower left and beyond a tan brick wall, two men in orange and gold stand on hexagonal paving with their heads inclined together, conferring. A blossoming tree and a cypress rise above the wall.
iconography: The gift platter is the picture's argument: patronage rendered as a transaction you can see. It is the single most reusable icon in the corpus for a game about court dependence.
The two figures outside the wall are the compositional counterweight — excluded from the audience, close enough to discuss it. Persian painting uses this device for gossip, conspiracy and witness.

The red tāj caps are Safavid dress, not Mamluk: the painter has costumed a c. 1390 Cairo event in the court fashion of his own 1560s Shiraz. The image documents how the memory was worn, not what the room looked like.

research.claim: Akhlāṭī was summoned to Cairo to serve as personal physician to Sultan Barqūq — which is precisely the relationship this painting depicts.
Under Akhlāṭī's influence Barqūq developed a keen interest in the occult sciences, as his personal library and his choice of courtiers suggest — and those courtiers included Ibn Turka himself.
Melvin-Koushki asks whether Barqūq was the first Mamluk sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and so an inspiration to Timurid rivals; he answers 'likely so'.

Lettrism's trajectory into this court ran in three stages: the Ibn ʿArabian-Būnian science of the saints (ʿilm al-awliyāʾ) in the 13th century, de-esotericized and adabized through the Mamluk literary-political mainstream in the 14th, then neopythagoreanized by the occultists who would form the Brethren at the turn of the 15th.
Ibn Turka's first major work, the Persian Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-durar, was completed in 1404 toward the end of his Cairo residence, and timuridizes the Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre.

images.description: A wall painting in a corner of the museum, running up to the ceiling beside a carved wooden door. Ulugh Beg stands at the centre in a plumed white turban and a gold-embroidered robe over a tan patterned coat with a worked belt, holding a brass astrolabe in both hands and looking out of the picture. To his left a bearded scholar in a gold-shouldered olive robe holds a bound book. At the lower right a young apprentice in pale blue kneels on a mat, marking a celestial globe on a turned stand with a stylus, an open book-box beside him. Behind them rises the white façade of the observatory, arcaded and arched, with the semicircular housing of the meridian arc breaking its roofline. Cypresses and pink blossoming branches flank the building; a lattice fence encloses a rose garden. The floor is a green star-pattern tile; a brass candlestick burns at the left. The sky is pale blue with a moon and faint stars. The whole is framed by a blue-and-gold border cartouche, with a geometric star-tile dado below.
iconography: Three registers of the same activity: the sultan holds the instrument, the scholar holds the book, the boy does the work. It is a picture of a research programme, with the labour at the bottom.
The astrolabe in a ruler's own hands is the whole claim of the sultan-scientist — this is not a prince being shown a discovery, it is a prince taking a measurement.
The lit candle under a night sky is the standard visual shorthand for observation carried through the night, and the only warm colour in an otherwise cool picture.

research.claim: Ulugh Beg was awarded the title al-sulṭān al-faylasūf, the philosopher-sultan.
research.source: Fazlıoğlu, Mathematical-Astronomical School, 41, cited in Melvin-Koushki, Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists, 3 n.9

research.claim: The mathematicalization of the occult sciences in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the members of the Samarkand Observatory — processes previously studied in atomistic isolation.

The model established by Iskandar Sulṭān and Ulugh Beg ensured that astronomy-astrology and lettrism in particular would continue to be heavily patronized by subsequent Timurid and Indo-Timurid dynasts, and by their Safavid and Ottoman competitors.

Ulugh Beg's star tables were updated two centuries later as the Zīj-i Shāhjahānī, which carries the first preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be explicitly and thoroughgoingly lettrist in tenor.
The observatory broke ground in 1420, the same year Ibn Turka completed the Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ (823/1420).

images.description: A palace of impossible architecture fills the whole folio: pink and salmon walls, orange staircases that turn at angles no stair turns at, balconies cantilevered over nothing, doors on every storey, each landing tiled in a different pattern of lapis, turquoise, white and gold. Near the top, in a small white-walled chamber, Yūsuf in a green robe strides left with one arm flung upward, a golden flame-halo around his head; Zulaykha in orange leans after him with a hand on his skirt. Gold cartouches of nastaʿlīq verse are set into the architecture at the top, at the middle left and along the foot, following the wall planes rather than the page. The margin is cream flecked with gold. Nothing in the building is structurally possible and every surface is finished to the same degree of attention.
iconography: The seven locked doors of the Qur'anic and Biblical story are distributed through the architecture; in the narrative they open of their own accord for Yūsuf, so the picture's real subject is a barrier that fails to hold.
The building is not a building. Its stairs, planes and openings are mutually contradictory, which makes it a diagram of a passage through levels rather than a depiction of a house.
Yūsuf's flame-halo marks prophetic status and is the only light source in a picture with no modelled light — illumination as ontological rank rather than as optics.

research.claim: Reading the impossible architecture as a cosmological diagram — an ascent through graded levels rather than a room — is directly compatible with the Ibn Turka material: the barzakh is precisely the intermediate domain through which forms pass between the intelligible and the sensible.
research.source: inference, consistent with the portal entries barzakh and imaginal-realm

research.claim: Ted's note on the file ('pure Ibn Turkian … a psychedelic out-of-body philosophy') reads the picture as an image of the soul's escape from the material. The imaginal realm (ʿālam al-khiyāl) is the technical term for the domain such a passage would occur in.
research.source: curatorial note by Ted Hand; concept per Melvin-Koushki, Being with a Capital B

research.claim: No hits for 'Zulaykha' or 'Bihzād' anywhere in the 43-source corpus — this image's connection to the Ibn Turka material is thematic and interpretive, not one Melvin-Koushki draws.

Sa'di's Bustan describes no palace. The seven-chambered building comes from Jami's Yusuf u Zulaykha, completed at Herat in 1483 - five years before this folio and in the same city - where the doors give way at the touch of Yusuf's pointing finger.
research.source: art-historical literature on the Cairo Bustan; see games/yusuf-ascent/data/research.json

research.claim: Recent work reads this folio's architectural inscriptions as encomiums of the painter rather than eulogies of the patron, making the Cairo Bustan central to arguments about the emergence of the named artist in late Timurid painting.
research.source: Balafrej, The Making of the Artist in Late Timurid Painting (2019) - not in hand; lead, not citation
